title: Borrower Restructuring Invalidates Guaranty Entity Reference
scenario:
**FIS Horizon — Loan System (Loan #CL-2024-08817)**
Borrower: Bridgewater Industrial Partners LLC | Commitment: $4.2M revolving line | Risk Rating: 5 (Pass) | Outstanding: $2.8M | Maturity: 09/2027
Guarantor(s): Bridgewater Holdings Inc. (unlimited personal guaranty executed 03/2022)
Covenant compliance: DSCR 1.25x minimum (last tested 12/2025: 1.31x) | LTV max 75% (current: 68%)

**Dynamics 365 — Customer Record**
Entity: 'Bridgewater Industrial Partners LLC' | Primary Contact: Marcus Devlin, CFO
Related Entities: 'Bridgewater Holdings Inc.' (parent — INACTIVE since 07/2025), 'Bridgewater Capital Group Inc.' (new parent — created 08/2025)
Note (08/15/2025, @r.martinez): 'Customer restructured. Holdings dissolved into new parent entity per their counsel. Updated D365 linkage.'

**SharePoint — /credit-memos/bridgewater/ (Credit Memo dated 03/2022)**
Approval: SVP Commercial Lending (J. Okafor)
Section 4 — Guaranty Structure: 'Unlimited continuing guaranty from Bridgewater Holdings Inc., the 100% parent of borrower. Guaranty to remain in effect for duration of facility regardless of changes in ownership structure per Section 8(c) of guaranty agreement.'

**Microsoft Teams — #commercial-lending-ops (09/12/2025, 3:47 PM)**
@sarah.mills: Legal flagged something on the Bridgewater file. The guaranty references 'Bridgewater Holdings Inc.' which technically no longer exists.
@tom.whitfield: Did they do an assignment and assumption to the new parent?
@sarah.mills: Checking with outside counsel. Marcus said it was a 'simple conversion' not a dissolution.
@tom.whitfield: Big difference. If Holdings was dissolved, the guaranty may have terminated by operation of law.
@sarah.mills: 😬
[Thread — no further replies]

**Outlook — Email from external counsel (10/03/2025)**
From: j.brennan@kirklandpartners.com
To: s.mills@cascadefinancial.com
CC: legal-commercial@cascadefinancial.com
Subject: RE: Bridgewater Holdings — Entity Status

'Sarah — confirmed with NC Secretary of State. Bridgewater Holdings Inc. was administratively dissolved 07/01/2025. A new entity, Bridgewater Capital Group Inc., was formed 07/15/2025 with identical ownership. However, there was no formal assignment of the guaranty obligation. The successor entity argument is fact-dependent under NC law but the 2-week gap creates risk. Recommend obtaining a new guaranty or ratification from Capital Group. Happy to draft.'

**ServiceNow — Annual Review Workflow (CR-2025-4421)**
Status: In Progress | Assigned: S. Mills | Due: 12/15/2025
Task: Complete annual credit review for Bridgewater Industrial Partners
Comment (11/20/2025, @s.mills): 'Guaranty issue still unresolved. Leaving risk rating at 5 pending legal resolution.'
Comment (12/01/2025, @audit.team): 'Per loan policy 7.3, unsupported guaranty = immediate downgrade to Watch. Please confirm status or adjust rating by COB 12/10.'
question: The borrower has requested a $600K draw on the revolver, which would bring total outstanding to $3.4M. Given the current state of the guaranty, the entity restructuring, and applicable credit policy, what is the correct course of action?
choices: A) Escalate to SVP for exception approval since the original approving officer (J. Okafor) is still on staff and can authorize continued advances under the existing commitment
B) Decline the draw until a new guaranty or ratification is obtained from Bridgewater Capital Group Inc., and downgrade the risk rating to Watch per Policy 7.3
C) Approve the draw — the guaranty's Section 8(c) survives changes in ownership structure, and the DSCR and LTV covenants are in compliance
D) Approve the draw — Bridgewater Capital Group is the legal successor with identical ownership, so the guaranty transfers automatically under NC law
rationale: The outside counsel email is the critical signal: Bridgewater Holdings was dissolved (not converted), creating a 2-week gap before the new entity was formed, and no formal assignment of the guaranty occurred. This means the guaranty is legally unsupported regardless of Section 8(c) language, because the guarantor entity ceased to exist by operation of law — the clause protects against ownership changes, not entity dissolution. Additionally, the audit team's comment citing Policy 7.3 requires an immediate downgrade when the guaranty is unsupported, which would restrict new advances. Answer A incorrectly relies on Section 8(c), which addresses ownership changes, not entity dissolution. Answer C incorrectly assumes automatic successor liability — outside counsel specifically noted this is 'fact-dependent' and the gap creates risk. Answer D is procedurally irrelevant; the issue isn't approval authority but the legal validity of the credit support structure.

title: Verbal Commitment Under Prior Credit Policy During Mid-Cycle Tightening
scenario:
**FIS Horizon — Pipeline Report (as of 11/15/2025)**
Loan #PENDING-2025-1134 | Borrower: Greystone Development Corp | Type: Construction-to-Perm | Amount: $8.5M | LTV: 78% | DSCR (projected): 1.18x | Status: Credit Memo in Progress
Relationship Manager: D. Parsons | Submitted to Credit: 10/28/2025

**SharePoint — Credit Policy Manual (Version 11.0, effective 11/01/2025)**
Section 3.2 — CRE Construction Lending:
'Maximum LTV for construction loans: 75%. Minimum DSCR (stabilized): 1.25x. No exceptions without Chief Credit Officer approval and documented mitigants.'
[Version History: v10.0 (effective 04/2023) stated: 'Maximum LTV: 80%. Minimum DSCR: 1.15x.']

**Outlook — Email Chain (10/22/2025)**
From: d.parsons@cascadefinancial.com
To: m.greystone@greystonedev.com
CC: t.whitfield@cascadefinancial.com
Subject: Cascade — Greystone Construction Facility

'Marcus — good speaking with you today. Per our discussion, we're pleased to confirm Cascade's interest in providing the $8.5M construction facility on the terms we discussed. I'll have the credit memo submitted by end of month. Formal commitment letter to follow after credit approval. Looking forward to partnering on this one.'

**Microsoft Teams — #cre-lending (10/30/2025, 11:22 AM)**
@d.parsons: Heads up — Greystone memo is in the queue. Tom gave verbal on this at 78% LTV back in October. Should be straightforward.
@j.chen: Policy 3.2 changed yesterday. New max LTV is 75% for construction. You aware?
@d.parsons: Wait what? That wasn't announced until the monthly.
@j.chen: Credit committee pushed it through 10/31 effective 11/1. The memo came out late Friday.
@d.parsons: We told the customer we'd do this. Tom was on the email.
@j.chen: 🤷‍♂️ talk to Tom

**SharePoint — Credit Committee Minutes (10/15/2025)**
[RESOLVED COMMENT by @cco.office, 10/29/2025]: 'Board approved tightening CRE parameters given market conditions. Transition guidance: loans with issued commitment letters prior to 11/1 are grandfathered. Pipeline deals without formal commitments subject to new policy.'

**Dynamics 365 — Relationship Notes (Greystone Development Corp)**
Entry (10/23/2025, D. Parsons): 'Verbal commitment extended per discussion with VP Whitfield. Customer expects formal CL within 3 weeks. Strong relationship — 3 prior deals closed, no losses. Greystone indicated competing term sheet from First National at 80% LTV.'

**Bloomberg Terminal — Market Data (pulled 11/10/2025)**
Greystone Development Corp — Private. No public filings.
Local CRE market (Charlotte MSA): Cap rate compression; office vacancy 14.2% (up from 11.8% YoY). Construction cost index +6.3% YTD.
question: Given the policy change, the verbal commitment, and the transition guidance in the credit committee minutes, what is the correct path for the Greystone $8.5M construction loan?
choices: A) Honor the verbal commitment at 78% LTV — the email from 10/22 with a VP on CC constitutes an institutional commitment that predates the policy change
B) Apply new Policy 3.2 (75% LTV, 1.25x DSCR) — the transition guidance explicitly states only loans with issued commitment letters are grandfathered, and no commitment letter was issued
C) Approve at 78% LTV under the old policy since the credit memo was submitted on 10/28, one day before the new policy was approved by credit committee
D) Restructure to 75% LTV to comply with new policy but offer a rate concession to preserve the relationship, since the competing term sheet from First National makes this a retention risk
rationale: The resolved comment in the Credit Committee Minutes contains the decisive transition guidance: 'loans with issued commitment letters prior to 11/1 are grandfathered. Pipeline deals without formal commitments subject to new policy.' The email from Parsons explicitly states 'formal commitment letter to follow after credit approval' — meaning no commitment letter was ever issued. A verbal commitment and an interest email do not constitute a formal commitment letter under banking practice. The credit memo submission date (10/28) is irrelevant because the grandfathering clause keys on the commitment letter issuance, not memo submission. Answer A incorrectly elevates a relationship manager's email to the status of a binding institutional commitment — it explicitly says the formal CL is pending. Answer C incorrectly focuses on the memo submission date rather than the commitment letter criterion in the transition guidance. Answer D represents a reasonable business strategy but is not the correct policy interpretation — it assumes discretion where the new policy requires CCO exception approval, which hasn't been sought.

title: Departed Officer's Modification Approval Against Updated Delegation Matrix
scenario:
**FIS Horizon — Loan Modification Record (Loan #CL-2023-06290)**
Borrower: Meridian Logistics Group LLC | Original Commitment: $6.0M term loan | Current Outstanding: $4.1M
Modification Date: 06/15/2025 | Type: Covenant waiver + amortization extension
Modification Details: Waived DSCR covenant (1.20x minimum) for Q2/Q3 2025; extended amortization from 20yr to 25yr; reduced quarterly principal from $75K to $60K.
Approving Officer: R. Hargrove, SVP Commercial Lending
Risk Rating: 6 (Special Mention)

**Workday — HR Record**
Robert Hargrove | Title at termination: SVP, Commercial Lending | Termination date: 08/30/2025 | Reason: Voluntary resignation
Delegation of Authority (at time of departure): Up to $5.0M for standard modifications; up to $3.0M for classified asset modifications (Risk Rating 6+)

**SharePoint — Delegation of Authority Matrix (Version 3.2, effective 03/01/2025)**
SVP, Commercial Lending:
- Standard modifications (Risk Rating 1-5): Up to $5.0M
- Classified asset modifications (Risk Rating 6-8): Up to $3.0M
- Modifications involving covenant waivers on classified assets: Up to $2.0M (requires co-approval from Credit Risk Officer)
[Version 2.8 (effective 01/2024) stated: 'SVP authority for all modification types: Up to $5.0M']

**Microsoft Teams — #credit-risk (06/10/2025, 2:15 PM)**
@r.hargrove: Running a mod through on Meridian Logistics — covenant waiver plus amor extension. Total exposure $4.1M, rated 6. Need anything from your side?
@k.patel (Credit Risk Officer): What's the total mod value? Is this just the waiver or are we looking at economic impact of the amor change?
@r.hargrove: Waiver is temporary (2 quarters). Amor extension reduces payment by $15K/qtr. Total economic concession maybe $200K NPV?
@k.patel: Should be fine. 👍
[No further messages in thread]

**Outlook — Email (09/15/2025)**
From: audit-findings@cascadefinancial.com
To: t.whitfield@cascadefinancial.com; chief.credit.officer@cascadefinancial.com
Subject: Loan Modification Audit — Q2/Q3 2025 Sample

'During our sample review of loan modifications, we identified Loan #CL-2023-06290 (Meridian Logistics) as potentially exceeding the approving officer's delegated authority. Under DOA Matrix v3.2 (effective 03/2025), covenant waivers on classified assets require Credit Risk Officer co-approval with a $2.0M cap. The modification was on a $4.1M classified asset. Please confirm proper authorization was obtained.'

**ServiceNow — Audit Response Tracking (AR-2025-0087)**
Status: Open | Due: 10/15/2025 | Assigned: T. Whitfield
Comment (09/18/2025, @t.whitfield): 'Reviewing. Hargrove departed 08/30. Need to determine if Teams exchange with Patel constitutes co-approval.'
Comment (09/22/2025, @compliance.review): 'DOA Matrix requires co-approval to be documented in the credit file. A Teams thumbs-up does not meet documentation standards per Policy 12.1(b). However, if Patel confirms intent, a retroactive memo may cure the deficiency.'
question: Regarding the audit finding on the Meridian Logistics modification: was the modification validly approved, and what remediation (if any) is required?
choices: A) The modification was validly approved — Hargrove had $5.0M authority for all modification types under the DOA Matrix that was current when the loan was originally booked (v2.8)
B) The modification was validly approved — Patel's thumbs-up in Teams constitutes co-approval from the Credit Risk Officer, satisfying the DOA Matrix v3.2 two-signature requirement
C) The modification is void and must be unwound — Hargrove acted outside his authority on a classified asset, making the covenant waiver and amortization extension unenforceable

D) The modification exceeded Hargrove's authority and the Teams thumbs-up from Patel does not constitute valid co-approval; the modification must be re-ratified by an officer with proper authority and a retroactive credit memo must be filed
rationale: The DOA Matrix v3.2 (effective 03/2025) is the operative version at the time of the modification (06/2025). Under this version, covenant waivers on classified assets (Risk Rating 6+) have a $2.0M cap and require Credit Risk Officer co-approval. The Meridian modification at $4.1M exceeds the $2.0M cap regardless of co-approval. Furthermore, the compliance review comment in ServiceNow explicitly states that a Teams thumbs-up does not meet documentation standards per Policy 12.1(b) — but also notes that a retroactive memo from Patel could cure the deficiency. The modification itself isn't void (Answer A is wrong — banks don't unwind modifications due to internal authority gaps; they remediate documentation), but it does need proper ratification. Answer A incorrectly applies the old DOA Matrix v2.8, which was superseded 3 months before the modification. Answer C incorrectly treats an informal emoji as meeting the formal co-approval documentation requirement. Answer A overstates the consequence — internal delegation breaches require remediation, not unwinding of customer-facing agreements.
